rv.q: It makes a play about imaginative as well as physical endurance.

The ensuing nightmare becomes vividly believable. Your heart is in your mouth as Josh Williams and Angus Yellowlees clamber across this perilous terrain; more importantly still, you empathise with them as they confront an impossible moral dilemma.
Their breathlessly exciting production, first staged at Bristol Old Vic, conjures wide-open landscapes and vertiginous drops.
What elevates 'Touching the Void' from 'well-judged' to 'spine-tingling' is Morris's exemplary staging, in cahoots with a crack creative team.

What the production does particularly well, however, is make it possible to appreciate Simon's horrific predicament in leaving his climbing partner behind while also allowing the audience to marvel at human resilience in the most testing of circumstances.
What it is, though, is a thrillingly original spectacle that's also highly informative about 'Alpine-style' mountaineering.

It shouldn’t work. Attempting to make effective theatre out of scaling a mountain, facing disaster thousands of feet up in the freezing cold and enduring a drawn-out facedown with death is surely a preposterous idea. Yet that is exactly what playwright David Grieg and director Tom Morris and his ideally meshed creative team have done.
It's also a penetrating portrayal of the impulse of human survival, against the odds: a thrilling, salutary reminder of our shared humanity and ability to overcome hardships, however extreme.
As an affirmation of the human spirit, Touching the Void is great, but it doesn't quite scale the summit.
But neither figure was present on the mountain so their talk feels like a distraction from the key drama.

cn.t: Critics hail this audacious stage adaptation as spellbinding and dramatically excellent, with Greig and Morris brilliantly translating Simpson's harrowing mountain survival story to the stage despite the seeming impossibility of the task.
